title: setuid: the most dangerous bit on the filesystem
objective: By the end of this course you can audit a system's setuid programs, explain three distinct ways they are attacked, and rewrite one to hold the least privilege that still does its job.

blocks.text: Everything in this course meets here. setuid is a single bit that makes a program run with the file owner's identity rather than the caller's — the mechanism behind passwd, mount, and su. It is also where a large share of local privilege escalation lives, because it hands a program written by one person the authority of another, in an environment the attacker controls.

blocks.caption: Verified: the same binary, before and after
lines: $ chmod 755 idtest ; ./idtest
real uid=1000  effective uid=1000
$ chown root idtest && chmod 4755 idtest
$ ls -l idtest
-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ... idtest        <- the s replaces the owner's x
$ ./idtest                                (still run by uid 1000)
real uid=1000  effective uid=0          <- identity changed
CapEff: 00000000a80425fb                <- and it received nearly every capability

blocks.text: Real uid stays as the caller — that is who invoked it. Effective uid becomes the owner, and that is what permission checks use. The capability set is the part people forget: the program did not ask for the ability to load kernel modules or change any file's owner, but it received both.
Attack one: the environment is the attacker's

A setuid program inherits the environment of whoever ran it, and an attacker chooses that environment completely. PATH is the classic lever: if the program runs another command by name, the attacker decides which file that name resolves to.

blocks.caption: Measured, on a deliberately vulnerable program that calls system("id")
lines: # normal PATH
uid=1000(tester) gid=1000(tester)
# attacker's directory placed first in PATH
[ATTACKER CODE RAN] real=1000 effective=1000
# The attacker's file named 'id' was executed instead of the real one.

blocks.title: Note what did NOT happen — and why it is not reassuring
blocks.text: The attacker's code reported effective uid 1000, not 0. Modern shells drop setuid privilege when they start with effective uid different from real uid, so system() did not hand over a root shell. That is a useful defence, and it is not a reason to relax: the attacker still achieved arbitrary code execution inside a privileged program's flow, and any privileged action the program takes afterwards is still taken. Defence in depth means the outer wall held; it does not mean the gate was locked.

items: Never use system() or popen() in a privileged program — they invoke a shell, which parses what you pass it
Use execve with an absolute path and an environment you constructed, not the one you inherited
Reset the environment: sanitise or clear PATH, IFS, LD_PRELOAD, LD_LIBRARY_PATH before doing anything
The dynamic linker already ignores LD_PRELOAD for setuid binaries — do not rely on that being the only such variable

blocks.text: This is the race condition from module three, in its security form. A privileged program checks whether the caller may use a path, and then opens it. Between the two steps the attacker replaces the path with a symlink to something else, and the privileged open follows it.

blocks.caption: The wrong shape, and the right one
lines: /* WRONG: two operations on a name, with a window between them */
if (access(path, W_OK) == 0) {      /* checks with the REAL uid */
FILE *f = fopen(path, "a");     /* opens with the EFFECTIVE uid */
/* The attacker swaps 'path' for a symlink during the window. */
/* RIGHT: drop privilege and let the kernel check once, atomically */
seteuid(getuid());                  /* now act as the caller */
int fd = open(path, O_WRONLY | O_APPEND | O_NOFOLLOW);
/* One operation. No window. O_NOFOLLOW refuses a symlink outright. */

blocks.title: access() exists almost entirely for this bug
blocks.text: It answers 'could the real uid do this?' — a question that is only interesting to a setuid program, and one whose answer is stale the moment it returns. If you find access() in privileged code, you have almost certainly found this defect. Act with the right identity and let the single operation succeed or fail.
Attack three: everything the program does on your behalf

items: It writes a file whose path you supplied — you point it at something you should not be able to write
It reads a file and shows you an error containing part of the contents
It passes your argument to a format string, or to a buffer sized for smaller input — the C course's bugs, now with root's authority
It spawns a helper that inherits its privilege

blocks.text: The unifying rule: in a privileged program, every input is hostile — arguments, environment, file contents, the current directory, resource limits, even the set of open file descriptors it was started with.
Two facts that will save you time

First, verified: setting the setuid bit on a shell script does nothing. A script with mode -rwsr-xr-x ran with uid 1000, because Linux ignores the bit on interpreted files — the race between reading the shebang and the interpreter opening the file was unfixable, so the feature was removed. If you need a privileged helper, it must be a compiled binary, or a properly configured sudo rule.

Second, the list is short and worth knowing. On a minimal Debian system the setuid binaries were: chsh, mount, chfn, gpasswd, umount, passwd, su, newgrp. That is the entire privileged attack surface of that install. On your own machines, that list is a security inventory you should be able to justify line by line.

items: First ask whether a file capability would do instead — ping needs cap_net_raw, not root, as the previous lesson verified
Drop privilege as early as possible, and permanently with setresuid when you will not need it again
Hold it only around the one operation that requires it
Use absolute paths for every file and every program you execute
Construct the environment you pass on; never forward the one you were given
Validate every argument against what you expect, not against what you know is bad
Keep the program small — this is the one place where lines of code are directly a risk measure

blocks.title: Audit, exploit, and then fix
steps: Run: find /usr/bin /usr/sbin /bin /sbin -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null    and list your machine's setuid programs
For each, write one sentence on what privileged thing it needs — and check with getcap whether it uses capabilities instead
Write a small setuid-root program that calls system("id"), and run it as a normal user
Create a directory containing an executable named id, put it first in PATH, and run the program again — confirm your file ran
Now replace system() with execve("/usr/bin/id", ...) and a constructed environment; confirm the attack no longer works
Write the access()-then-fopen() version, and race it by swapping the path for a symlink during the window
Rewrite it with seteuid plus a single open(O_NOFOLLOW) and confirm the race is gone
Finally: chmod 4755 a shell script and confirm the bit is ignored
blocks.expected: An inventory you can justify, an exploit you built yourself, and two fixes that remove it structurally rather than by luck. If you can explain to someone else why the second version cannot be attacked the same way — not that it is harder, but why the window no longer exists — you have finished this course.

cheatsheet: setuid runs a program with the file owner's effective uid; ls shows s in place of the owner's x
Verified: setuid root gave effective uid 0 AND capability set a80425fb
Real uid stays the caller's; effective uid is what permission checks use
The environment belongs to the attacker: PATH, IFS, LD_* — clear or construct it
Never system() or popen() in a privileged program; execve an absolute path
Measured: a PATH-injected file was executed by a setuid program's system() call
Modern shells drop setuid privilege, which limits that attack but does not remove it
access() then open() is the classic TOCTOU bug — drop privilege and do one atomic operation
O_NOFOLLOW refuses to follow a symlink
Verified: Linux ignores the setuid bit on shell scripts entirely
A minimal Debian had 8 setuid binaries: chsh, mount, chfn, gpasswd, umount, passwd, su, newgrp
Prefer a file capability; drop privilege early and permanently; keep the program small

checkpoint.prompt: A setuid-root program calls system("grep ..."). An attacker puts their own grep first in PATH. What do they achieve?

choices.B: Their code executes inside the privileged program's flow; modern shells drop setuid privilege, but the program's own privileged actions still happen
choices.C: An immediate root shell in all cases

checkpoint.explanation: Verified: the injected file ran, reporting effective uid 1000 because the shell dropped privilege. That mitigation is real and is not a licence to use system() — the attacker still got code execution inside a privileged process.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is access() followed by fopen() a security bug in a setuid program?

choices.B: The check and the use are separate operations on a name, and the attacker can swap what that name refers to in between
choices.C: fopen cannot open files owned by root

checkpoint.explanation: It is module three's race condition with privilege attached. The fix is not a smaller window — it is dropping privilege and performing one atomic operation.

checkpoint.prompt: You add the setuid bit to a shell script owned by root. What happens when a normal user runs it?

choices.B: It runs as the calling user — Linux ignores the setuid bit on interpreted files
choices.D: It runs as root only if the shebang is absolute

checkpoint.explanation: Verified: a script with mode -rwsr-xr-x reported uid 1000. The feature was removed because the gap between reading the shebang and the interpreter opening the file could not be closed.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the first question to ask about a program that currently needs setuid root?

choices.B: Which single privileged ability does it actually need, and would a file capability grant just that
choices.C: Can we hide it from users
choices.D: Should it be written in a different language

checkpoint.explanation: That is the measured difference from the previous lesson: capability set 2000 instead of a80425fb. Same functionality, a fraction of the authority to lose.
